newsitem.title: JAPAN: Rate hike fears threaten Japan bond 'bubble'.
newsitem.headline: Rate hike fears threaten Japan bond 'bubble'.

text.p: Japan's bond boom, supported by what one official called "negative exuberance", may be coming to an end as traders start to take serious the warning that the current low interest rates will not continue indefinitely.
Government officials and business leaders raised the stakes in the past week, saying the environment was changing to one which would allow for a rise in interest rates.

"Long-term interest rates (in Japan) have been abnormally low, given the strength of the underlying economy, while the negative aspects of the Bank of Japan's ultra-easy money policy are surfacing," said Shoji Kitta, president of Totan Research Co Ltd.

One of the negative aspects emerged on Friday morning when the Ministry of Finance (MOF) announced it had ordered Nissan Mutual Life Insurance Co to halt all operations except for servicing current customers, the first time the government has forced an insurer to shut down in the postwar period.

The MOF said low interest rates and a stagnant Japanese stock market exposed the medium-size insurer to a large gap between investment returns and the payouts it guaranteed on special high-yielding policies it pushed aggressively during the "bubble economy" era of inflated asset prices in the late 1980s.
The BOJ slashed the official discount rate (ODR), which it charges on overnight loans to commercial banks, to a record low 0.5 percent in September 1995.
"The ultra-easy credit is a double-edged sword. It promises handsome operating profits for ailing banks, but is hurting institutional investors," Kitta said.
Changing market sentiment could drive up the benchmark Japanese government bond (JGB) yield to 2.7-2.8 percent in the medium term, he added.
The key bond yield shot up by 0.13 percentage point to 2.285 percent on Friday after the announcement of Nissan Mutual Life's business suspension.
The yield hit a record low of 2.075 percent on April 8.

Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of MOF's International Finance Bureau, warned on April 18 that the JGB market is considerably "bubbly" and he sees the risk of a bursting of the "negative exuberance".
"Current (long-term) interest rate levels are abnormal and it would be natural if those levels were to be normalised in the future," he said.
Mamoru Yamasaki, senior economist at Paribas Capital Markets, predicted that the JGB yield would rise to 2.5 percent to 3.0 percent in the latter half of this year.
The BOJ has also started to sound the alarm about possible rising prices amid the backdrop of the yen's recent weakness.
In its quarterly economic outlook on Friday, the central bank said prices in Japan have stopped declining and attention to exchange rates was required in regard to prices.

Consumer prices in central Tokyo in April climbed 1.7 percent from March due to an increase in the consumption tax rate, the Management and Coordination Agency said, adding the price rise was the highest in 17 years.
"The BOJ has already lost two main factors to justify the record low discount rate," said a senior fund manager at an investment advisory firm.
He said the the BOJ cut its official discount rate in 1995 in a bid to avoid a deflationary spiral and a further strengthening of the yen.
The yen has now fallen 60 percent from its peak of 79.75 to the dollar set in April 1995, while the BOJ now needs to watch upward pressure on prices, the fund manager said.
Toyoo Gyohten, a senior adviser to the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd, said on Thursday that the economic recovery was now able to withstand an interest rate rise.

"I think it's about time we start reviewing current interest rates. The Japanese economic recovery is not so weak that it will all of a sudden collapse if there is a rate rise," said Gyohten, who is also former vice finance minister for international affairs.
Traders said that the BOJ may let the call rate move above the ODR in late May or early June if it confirms the sales tax hike had only a limited impact on the economy.
On Friday, the BOJ said the extent of the negative effects of sales tax rise had yet to be confirmed.
